paragraphs: Amazon Data Services, also known as Amazon Web Services, is asking Indiana County, Pennsylvania, to approve 39 data centers on about 2,200 acres of the Homer City Energy Campus, the site of the former Homer City Generating Station coal plant. Power would come from FirstEnergy, backed by a new 4.5-gigawatt natural gas plant on the same property; the Mountain Watershed Association says that plant's wastewater permit would send 6.84 million gallons a day into Blacklick Creek, a trout-stocked stream, without covering the data centers themselves. More than 100 people attended the county planning commission's Sept. 9, 2026 meeting, and the commission tabled the plan while it keeps asking questions.

In Virginia, the company's Warrenton data center, a 220,000-square-foot building at Blackwell Road and Lee Highway, has been in court for more than three years. The town council approved it 4-3 after a hearing hundreds of residents attended to oppose it, and Citizens for Fauquier County sued in 2023 to void the approval. Judge Stephen Sincavage heard final arguments on June 15, 2026 and had not ruled by early August; Warrenton itself has since barred data centers from industrial districts and told the court it no longer shares Amazon's "litigation alignment."

In Prince William County, Amazon paid $218 million for the former Parsons Farm site on Dumfries Road, about 90 acres in Independent Hill, after supervisors voted 5-1 to let buildings there rise to 85 feet instead of 45. "It's time to say no to data centers," said Rachel Ellis of Gainesville. In September 2026 the county's supervisors voted 8-0 to end by-right data center development countywide, requiring a special use permit for new projects; Amazon's own site, with an approved plan, stays in the overlay district.

atNorth's two biggest projects on record are still being developed. SWE04 is a data center campus proposed for Hamre Industrial Park in Långsele, Sollefteå Municipality, Sweden, planned to run up to 300 megawatts of power; the company confirmed the plan in February 2026 and expects it operating in the first half of 2028. NOR01, in Tysvær, Norway, on a 36-hectare plot inside the Haugaland Business Park, would open with 120 megawatts and grow to 350 megawatts, with power projected for 2028.

Sollefteå Municipality says it sold atNorth the roughly 50-hectare Hamre plot for 175 million kronor, based on an independent valuation, and expects the project to create 100 to 150 direct jobs. A full environmental review, run by the company and the county administrative board, is still needed before construction starts, and the municipality handles building permits. "We are very pleased that atNorth has chosen Hamre Industrial Park for this significant investment," said Sollefteå mayor Emelie Wrede.

In Norway, park owner Haugaland Næringspark says atNorth aims to invest about NOK 11 billion in NOR01's first phase, with two new substations built by grid operators Statnett and Fagne. atNorth's owner, Swiss investment manager Partners Group, agreed in February 2026 to sell the company to the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Equinix; atNorth says the sale does not change who is building these sites. The company's other site on record, ICE01 in Hafnarfjörður, Iceland, is already operating at 3.2 megawatts.

Cielo Digital Infrastructure's data center plan in Haines City, Polk County, Florida, is on hold because the city does not have the water to serve it. The Texas-based company asked for up to 150,000 gallons of drinking water a day for a site near Marion Road and State Road 544 East, on top of Haines City's own pending request to raise its water permit to 16.42 million gallons a day. "No data center has even come before our commission to approve or not approve," Deputy City Manager James Keene said. Resident Jule Cortez said the area already lacks water, and a data center using 150,000 gallons a day "doesn't make sense." Cielo plans a 300-megawatt campus on about 74 acres there, DCD reported.

In Cherokee County, South Carolina, Cielo announced in June 2025 a $2.1 billion campus of four buildings at Ford Road in Gaffney, up to 300 megawatts at full build-out and due to begin operating by the end of 2028. Cherokee County Council finalized tax incentives but would not give their size or length. Resident Allison Tracy told the council, "This is not opposition to growth. It is a request for transparency in responsible decision-making." Ken Moon, executive director of the Cherokee County Development Board, said the project would generate roughly a third of the county's budget in taxes, and that future data centers would have to bring their own power.

Cielo, founded in 2023 and owned by the Texas investment manager Arroyo Investors, sold an earlier campus in Culpeper County, Virginia, to Edgecore. Its website has also listed projects in New Lenox and Minooka, Illinois; Clarksville, Tennessee; and Des Moines, Iowa, DCD reported, but two of those are disputed locally. At an August 2026 New Lenox village board meeting, Mayor Baldermann said there was false information that a data center was coming to New Lenox: "This is not true and we are not entertaining any data centers." And Clarksville Now reported in September 2026 that no data centers were proposed in Montgomery County, Tennessee, even as the county studied new zoning rules for water, electricity and noise.

Comcast, the US cable company, runs small data centers for its own network rather than building large campuses for tenants. Its newest approved site is a former TD Bank branch at 92 West Main Street in Clinton, New Jersey, which the town's land use board approved for conversion into a data center. Comcast Cable will use the 2,170-square-foot building to house servers, install two generators, remove the drive-through, and will not staff it constantly.

In Moorestown, New Jersey, Comcast put its 650 Centerton Road office and data center, built in 2001 on 5.1 acres, up for sale to investors in a sale-leaseback deal; the building is or was the site of the Comcast Cybersecurity Operations Center. In Pennsylvania, its three-building Boot Road campus in West Chester houses data centers and back-office operations, where Comcast has installed energy monitoring toward a goal to double network energy efficiency by 2030.
Comcast has also filed plans with Texas regulators for a $7.5 million, 5,200-square-foot data center in Willis, Montgomery County, Texas.

DartPoints is a small edge colocation company that runs regional data centers in mid-sized US markets rather than hyperscale campuses. It began planning a network of micro data centers in 2012, and after private equity firm Astra Capital took a majority stake, it bought Metro Data Centers in Dublin, Ohio, outside Columbus, in October 2020, then Immedion in March 2021. The Dublin site has 22,000 square feet of technical space and sits about 20 miles from the cloud campuses of Facebook, Google and Amazon Web Services in New Albany, Data Center Frontier reported.

In Louisiana, DartPoints acquired Venyu and its three data centers, including an 87,000 square foot Tier III building in Shreveport that was once a Selber Brothers department store, bringing its portfolio to 11 data centers in 10 markets with 20MW of capacity, DCD reported. "Serving Edge markets is where our passion and expertise lie," chief executive Scott Willis said. Its Asheville, North Carolina site, AVL01, is in the Biltmore Park Technology Center, with 23,000 square feet of white space and 1.5 MW of utility power, according to the company.

In Asheville, the city council has imposed a one-year moratorium on new data center construction, joining about 30 North Carolina localities that have paused them while they write permanent rules; the city's land-use rules did not even define a data center. "I think we need to take a pause and make sure we put in measures that address all the concerns that we have as a community," Mayor Esther Manheimer said. In Caddo Parish, around Shreveport, the parish commission voted 6-4 on Aug. 31, 2026 against asking its planning commission to consider pausing data center construction, as Amazon Web Services plans a campus there.

DC Blox is suing Metro Nashville in federal court over its plan for a data center next to the Nashville Zoo. The company argues that Metro unlawfully stopped processing its permits under the city's temporary data center moratorium, even though it says the city's zoning administrator had found its permit applications had already vested. The Atlanta-based company had finalized a $23 million purchase of the 23.49-acre site at 648 Grassmere Park, where it filed for a building permit for a one-story, 10-megawatt, 69,220-square-foot data center; engineering reports indicate a second, three-story, 40-megawatt building could follow, for up to 50 megawatts in total.

A petition against the project gathered more than 160,000 signatures in two days. "Nobody asked for this," said Tony Zavitson of Glencliff Neighbors of South Nashville. A DC Blox spokesperson told DCD the site "is not a large AI-factory" and would use closed-loop or waterless cooling. On July 21, 2026 the Metro Council unanimously passed Davidson County's first zoning rules for data centers and a temporary moratorium on new ones.

Outside Atlanta, DC Blox plans a three-building hyperscale campus of up to 216 megawatts on about 53 acres on Farmer Road in Conyers, Rockdale County; the company says a hyperscale client will anchor the first phase. Rockdale County's data center moratorium, first imposed in January, was extended through October 9, 2026, after commissioners deferred the county's new data center rules to an October 6 meeting. In Indianapolis, the Metropolitan Development Commission approved a scaled-back, two-building DC Blox campus at the Thunderbird Commerce Center on July 15, 2026, with peak demand the company has put at about 80 to 100 megawatts; opponents had filed an appeal.

EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure, a Denver-based data center developer, is building its largest campus in Louisa County, Virginia, and in August 2026 filed with the US Army Corps of Engineers for the campus's second phase: three data center buildings and substations on 187 acres, affecting 4.2 acres of wetlands and more than 6,300 feet of stream channels.

EdgeCore bought the 697-acre site in the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park, next to Interstate 64, from Louisa County for $42 million in June 2025, for a roughly 1.1-gigawatt campus it says will cost about $17 billion, to be powered by Rappahannock Electric Cooperative.

Louisa District Supervisor Manning Woodward has said on a local radio show that the campus will be "behind the meter," generating its own power, possibly with gas on site; he said the county had received no plans and that small modular reactors were an option but "those are way off." Because the county's 2019 zoning made "utility service major" a by-right use, EdgeCore could build a generating plant without a local public approval process.

In Loudoun County, EdgeCore secured $1.5 billion in financing in April 2026 for two data centers in Sterling, totaling 685,000 square feet and 114 megawatts at full buildout. The first, AS01, is scheduled for initial occupancy in November 2026, and the second in July 2027. EdgeCore also operates a campus in Santa Clara, California.

Galaxy Digital, led by founder and CEO Mike Novogratz, has turned its Helios bitcoin mining campus in Dickens County, West Texas, into an AI data center site leased to CoreWeave; the campus is delivering about 200 MW to CoreWeave so far, with 1,630 MW approved and under a 15-year lease Galaxy says will bring in more than $1 billion a year on average. In July 2026 Galaxy announced a second Texas campus, Project Merlin, on 500 acres in McGregor, expected to reach 74 MW in its first phase before expanding through 2030.

Dickens County, population under 2,000, signed a $20.5 million payment-in-lieu-of-taxes deal with Galaxy in July 2025, including $2 million for housing. County Judge Kevin Brendle said the county is betting on the industry for the long term; Helios expects more than 100 permanent staff, with CoreWeave adding 50 or more.

In McGregor, the city council approved the sale of nearly 500 acres to a Galaxy subsidiary in a closed session on June 22, 2026, netting the city about $7.5 million; Galaxy expects the first phase to begin receiving power in 2028. Resident Dennis Fehler started a petition to remove Mayor Jim Lilley over the closed-door vote and past water violations tied to SpaceX engine testing nearby, and more than 60 people had signed it, the San Antonio Express-News reported.

H5 Data Centers, based in Denver, buys existing data centers and carrier hotels rather than building large new campuses. Its biggest site is the former Yahoo campus in the Town of Lockport, Niagara County, New York, bought for a reported $49 million in a sale-leaseback deal that closed on December 30, 2024; Yahoo still operates there under a five-year lease. The buildings use a passively air-cooled "chicken-coop" design, with two on-site substations offering up to 44 megawatts.

The Town of Lockport held a public hearing on August 5, 2026 on a local law setting an 18-month moratorium on data center permitting, backed by the Niagara County Planning Board even though the town had received no new data center requests. No result of that hearing has been published.

In February 2026 H5 and the investment firm Novacap formed HyscaleIX Data Centers, a joint venture that bought three carrier hotels from 365 Data Centers in Buffalo, Nashville and Tampa, each hosting its local internet exchange. "This transaction reflects our continued focus on disciplined acquisitions and operational excellence," said CEO Josh Simms. In Albuquerque, H5 bought 505 Marquette in 2022, a 225,000-square-foot downtown carrier hotel with 20 on-site carriers, and that year also bought seven Vxchnge data centers across the US.

Karis Critical, a Naples, Florida developer, had two Chicago-suburb data center plans stopped by residents in 2026. On July 1 it withdrew its request to rezone the 186-acre Plum Farms property in Hoffman Estates, after weeks of organizing by neighbors there and in South Barrington and Barrington Hills. "We heard the feedback clearly, including the call for a more specific plan before any rezoning," spokesman Patrick Skarr said. Village staff had discussed a data center with Karis for 18 months before it bought the land for $45 million in January 2025.

In Naperville, the city council voted 6-1 on January 20, 2026 to deny Karis's 145,000-square-foot, 36 megawatt data center on the former Lucent campus, overturning the plan commission's recommendation. Karis had already cut its plan from two buildings and 72 megawatts, and a petition against it gathered more than 5,000 signatures. Its attorney offered to halve the diesel generators from 24 to 12, but several dozen residents still spoke against it. Karis said it was "disappointed by the outcome of the vote."

Karis has since explored the 168-acre former BP campus in Naperville for a stand-alone data center of 100,000 to 125,000 square feet, though "we have no pending proposal for the 168-acre campus," spokesman Patrick Skarr said. In northwest Indiana, Karis has proposed up to nine buildings on 180 acres east of Deep River in Merrillville, an up to $900 million investment still seeking a zone change and power approval from NIPSCO.

Metrobloks won approval in April 2026 to build a data center on the site of a former drive-in theater in Indianapolis's Martindale-Brightwood neighborhood. The city's Metropolitan Development Commission rezoned the roughly 14-acre parcel at 2505 North Sherman Drive, vacant since 1983, for a $500 million, 72 megawatt data center with closed-loop cooling. Residents stopped traffic in a protest days before the company filed its rezoning petition in October 2025, citing utility costs, pollution and few long-term benefits for the neighborhood. "Data centers are being pushed into Black legacy neighborhoods like Martindale Brightwood," the group Protect Martindale Brightwood wrote.

In Southfield, Michigan, the city council voted 5-2 in December 2025, after nearly six hours of public comment, to approve Metrobloks' site plan for a 109,683-square-foot, 100 megawatt data center on 12.19 acres on Inkster Road between 11 Mile Road and Interstate 696. Most residents who spoke opposed it. "Why do we have to be the first one?" asked resident Lysa Davis. Jeff Mandel, the Los Angeles company's chief investment officer, said the project could bring 35 permanent jobs and would have noise and tree buffers with closed-loop cooling.

In March 2026 Metrobloks announced a $1.4 billion, three-building campus of 568,800 square feet on 29 acres at 2515 Old Hughes Road in Liberty, Missouri, north of Kansas City, where it secured planning permission in December for the first two-story building. Metrobloks focuses on AI-ready data centers at the edge of metro areas; its chief executive, Ernest Popescu, previously worked in data center development at Iron Mountain.

NorthPoint Development, a Kansas City real estate company better known for warehouses, has proposed data center campuses in three communities and met organized opposition in each. The most advanced is Project Hazelnut, a 15-building campus in the Humboldt Industrial Park in Hazle Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania. Township supervisors voted 3-0 in November 2025 to deny its land development plans, and the company and township are now in litigation over that vote. NorthPoint is still pursuing state permits for the site, which it says would use 616 of about 1,300 acres and cool servers in the hottest months with treated wastewater from the local sewer authority.

In Alabama, NorthPoint holds an option on about 687 acres near Wilsonville, in Shelby County, for a campus of 14 buildings with a projected peak demand of 1,008 megawatts, more than half the output of Alabama Power's nearby Gaston plant. Residents organized against it before any application was filed. In California, the company has filed to split a former chemical plant site in Modesto for a data center whose size and operator have not been disclosed; after a packed August 2026 council meeting, five of seven council members said they favored a moratorium on data centers.

NorthPoint has also won approval, in April 2025, to add data center buildings to the Keystone Trade Center it is redeveloping on former U.S. Steel land in Falls Township, Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Supervisors there unanimously approved revised plans covering up to 2 million square feet across ten buildings; the company says a non-disclosure agreement stops it from saying how many megawatts they would draw.

Oppidan is a Minnesota property development firm that has been building data centers since 2016, mostly smaller facilities for other companies. Its largest proposal, a campus near home in Apple Valley, Dakota County, was turned down. With landowner Rockport LLC, Oppidan proposed the Apple Valley Technology Park on gravel-mining land: five buildings totaling 1.05 million square feet and 250 to 300 megawatts. The city said the use conflicted with its comprehensive plan and that it could not supply the water the data center would need. After the council denied the plan amendment in January 2026, Oppidan and Rockport withdrew their rezoning requests in March, and the council unanimously denied the remaining approvals on March 26. On July 9, 2026, Apple Valley adopted a one-year moratorium on new data centers that halts any further consideration of the site.

Its smaller projects have fared better. In Beaver Dam, Dodge County, Wisconsin, the Common Council voted 11 to 3 in April 2026 to sell Oppidan 13 acres of city land for $407,340 for a 90,000-square-foot edge data center near Meta's much larger campus; construction was set to start in summer 2026. In Reno, the city council overturned its own planning commission in March 2025 to approve an Oppidan data center using 8 megawatts of power and 8 acre-feet of water a year, after the commission had denied it over water and power questions.

In Texas, Oppidan filed in 2024 for a $27.1 million, 5-megawatt data center in El Paso County. In Maryland it was the lead developer, with Harrison Street, of the Sandy Farms powered shell in Severn, Anne Arundel County, which Harrison Street sold with a Laurel site to GI Partners for a combined $221.9 million, Data Center Dynamics reported in March 2026. Data Center Dynamics also reported that Oppidan is building a 61,000-square-foot data center in Eagan, Minnesota, which has no page here yet.

Prologis, the California-based industrial real estate giant best known for warehouses, has moved into data centers, and its record is mixed. Its one campus under construction is Project Mila in Trenton, Butler County, Ohio, being built for Amazon Web Services on 141 acres Prologis bought from the city for $7.7 million: a 250-megawatt campus totaling 893,034 square feet. The Trenton Planning Commission approved the site plan unanimously in March 2026, and the city council later gave Prologis a Community Reinvestment Area agreement with a 75 percent property tax exemption on each building for 15 years. Residents organized against it, and after the Ohio Supreme Court ordered the council to certify their petition, Trenton voters will decide on November 3, 2026 whether to ban new data centers needing more than 25 megawatts. The ban would not affect the Prologis campus, which is already under way.

In Shelbyville, Shelby County, Indiana, the Common Council voted 4 to 2, with one abstention, in April 2026 to annex 429 acres and approve an economic development agreement for a Prologis campus of up to 11 buildings east of the State Road 44 and Interstate 74 interchange. Prologis gets a 30-year, 100 percent personal property tax abatement and a 10-year, 50 percent abatement on real property, and in return must spend at least $2 billion and create 25 jobs for each data center building. A Shelby Superior Court judge later ruled for the city in a lawsuit over the annexation and rezoning. The fight turned bitter in June, when a video showed Mayor Scott Furgeson saying he saw "No Data Centers" signs only at run-down houses; he later apologized, saying, "I take full responsibility for what I said."

Elsewhere Prologis has been turned away. In Kosciusko County, Indiana, the county commissioners voted 3 to 0 in April 2025 to uphold their plan commission's recommendation to deny rezoning more than 500 acres of farmland near Leesburg for a Prologis data center. "We're not against a data center. We're against a data center in this location," said Jack Birch, the attorney for the objectors. In Washington Township, Macomb County, Michigan, Prologis withdrew its application to rezone 312 acres on 32 Mile Road in a letter dated May 19, 2026, saying it would wait until the township adopts rules for data centers.

Prologis is also lined up to buy Project Sail, the 900-megawatt campus near Newnan in Coweta County, Georgia, from its developer Atlas Development; DCD reported in April 2026, when the county approved the rezoning, that Prologis had not yet closed on the purchase.

Related Digital is the data center arm of the New York real estate firm Related Companies, and it is building two of the most closely watched campuses in the country. The larger is the OpenAI and Oracle Stargate campus in Saline Township, Washtenaw County, Michigan, known locally as "The Barn": a $16 billion, 21-million-square-foot development expected to draw about 1.4 gigawatts from DTE Energy. Related bought the farmland from three landowners in May 2025. The township's planning commission and board rejected the rezoning in September 2025; two days later Related Digital and the landowners sued, alleging exclusionary zoning, and the township settled with a consent judgment requiring it to approve the project. Construction began that November. The Michigan Public Service Commission conditionally approved DTE's power contracts for the site in December 2025, making DTE responsible for any costs it cannot recover from the company.

The fight has since moved to taxes. In July 2026 the township board granted the 12-year, 50 percent abatement the settlement required but based it on the $4.8 billion valuation named in the settlement rather than the $43 billion the company had offered, a much smaller break; later that month the board voted 5 to 0 to remove the cap after its attorney warned it risked violating the consent judgment. In August resident Kathryn Haushalter and attorney Ellis Boal asked the Michigan State Tax Commission to deny the exemption, arguing the township never held the public hearing needed to create the industrial development district it depends on. Haushalter, who lives nearby, has described construction light glowing through her bedroom window before sunrise: "My kids are going to be outside breathing that," she said of the diesel backup generators.

Related's other campus is in Cheyenne, Laramie County, Wyoming, where it broke ground on October 7, 2025 on a $1.2 billion development for CoreWeave on 115 acres of the Cheyenne Business Parkway. CoreWeave leases the first 88 megawatts, in a 184,000-square-foot building due in late 2026, and the campus is planned for 302 megawatts; Cowboy State Daily later reported Related expects it eventually to deliver up to 420 megawatts. "We decided we will only build self-contained cooling systems that do not use water," Related Companies chief executive Jeff Blau said at the groundbreaking, where he also gave $3.5 million toward a city affordable housing project. By June 2026 more than 400 construction workers were on site.

Riot Platforms made its name mining bitcoin in Texas and is now turning its campuses into AI data centers. In August 2026 it disclosed a 20-year, $9.1 billion lease at its Rockdale campus in Milam County to supply 191 megawatts of computing capacity to what it called a "leading frontier AI lab"; Bloomberg identified the tenant as Anthropic. Riot said it would deliver 96 megawatts by December 2027 and all 191 by June 2028, and chief executive Jason Les said that deal and a smaller lease with AMD gave Riot about $9.8 billion in contracted data center revenue. Rockdale, on the site of a former Alcoa aluminum smelter, is Riot's flagship, with 700 megawatts of developed capacity. In January 2026 Riot bought the 200 acres under it for $96 million, paid for by selling about 1,080 bitcoin, and signed AMD for an initial 25 megawatts. Greenpeace has called Rockdale the most energy and carbon-intensive bitcoin mine in the United States.

Its other Texas campus, on FM 709 outside Corsicana in Navarro County, was energized in April 2024 and is meant to reach 1 gigawatt. In 2026 Riot filed to add Project Ditto, a $400 million, 335,430-square-foot data center building there, running from April 2026 to May 2028. The site has been fought over: in March 2024 Navarro County commissioners declined to act on a tax abatement for a $640 million expansion after residents flooded them with emails, texts and visits opposing it, and opponents organized as the Texas Coalition Against Cryptomining. The facility draws about 1.5 million gallons of water a day at peak summer use, The Nation reported.

Texas has since tightened the terms. On August 3, 2026 Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission and ERCOT to pause approvals for data centers seeking new grid connections until regulators audit their water use, power demand and tax incentives, and on August 18 his office said Riot had committed to comply with his standards, including paying for its own grid upgrades. In Kentucky, Riot owns a 60-megawatt mining center outside Paducah, bought with Block Mining in 2024, and said in May 2026 it would study pairing future data centers there with small nuclear reactors from Terrestrial Energy; no timeline has been released.

Soluna Holdings, based in Albany, New York, builds data centers for bitcoin mining and increasingly for AI beside wind, solar and hydroelectric plants, using power that would otherwise go to waste. As of August 1, 2026 it operated about 192 megawatts across three energized sites in Texas and Kentucky, with more under construction and a Texas pipeline it puts at about 6.3 gigawatts. In August 2026 it enlarged several projects for AI: Rosa grew from 187 to 242 megawatts, Hedy from 120 to 198, and Ellen, in Cameron County, from 100 to 145.

Its main campus is Dorothy, south of Silverton in Briscoe County, where two buildings run on the 150 megawatt Briscoe Wind Farm next door. Soluna bought the wind farm for $53 million in April 2026, then closed in August on 397 more acres for Dorothy 3, an AI campus of up to 300 megawatts. Briscoe County Judge Rank Cogdell said the site has "filled in a gap" left when the county lost tax abatement money from the wind farms, and commissioners are weighing an abatement for the larger plan.

In the Rio Grande Valley, Willacy County welcomes Project Kati for its taxable value, but neighboring Cameron County has said it will not offer data centers tax abatements and had received no permit applications as of May 2026. Since August 3, 2026, new data center connections to the Texas grid have been on hold while state regulators audit projects in the queue. In Kentucky, Calloway County's fiscal court took up a 12-month data center moratorium in July 2026 that would block any expansion of Soluna's existing bitcoin mine in Murray.

Western Hospitality Partners, or WHP, is a New York City-based data center developer. Little is published about the company itself, DCD has noted, but its name has been attached to proposals in Kentucky, Indiana, Pennsylvania, Illinois and Alabama. None of its Kentucky or Illinois projects has been built: two were withdrawn in Kentucky, one in Illinois was dropped, and one in Illinois is on hold.

Its largest plan, Project Lincoln, was announced in late March 2025 for 267 acres of farmland on Highway 53 in Oldham County, Kentucky: eight buildings, 2 million square feet and 600 megawatts, at a cost of $6 billion. Residents objected that WHP had applied as a "private utility" to put heavy industry on agricultural land without a rezoning vote by the elected fiscal court. On June 2, 2025 the company moved the plan to a 30-acre drive-in theater site nearby, with two buildings instead of eight. On July 1 the fiscal court passed a 150-day moratorium on all data centers with no exemption for projects already filed, and two days later WHP withdrew, saying the project "will be withdrawn and will not proceed."

In Illinois, WHP held an option to buy about 320 acres of Pekin's Lutticken Farm for $4.5 million. Opponents formed a Facebook group of more than 2,200 members and delivered about 2,000 petition signatures, and in March 2026 Mayor Mary Burress said the city would not move forward; in May WHP's lawyers terminated the agreement. Its remaining Illinois site is in Braidwood, near the 2.2-gigawatt Braidwood nuclear plant, where it is working with Found Digital on a campus of up to eight buildings; the developer has closed on the land, but in January 2026 the city said the project was on hold because of ComEd's infrastructure requirements.
In Kentucky, Oldham County's fiscal court is due to vote on permanent data center rules on October 6, 2026, including a 10-megawatt power cap that would effectively bar hyperscale data centers.

US Signal, a Grand Rapids, Michigan, company that provides network and data center services, runs four sites tracked here: one each in Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, plus its second Indianapolis facility at 6325 Morenci Trail, a 9,600-square-foot, 2-megawatt building bought from local operator Rack Bunker in December 2023.

Its owner, Igneo Infrastructure Partners, is funding a $200 million program adding 3 megawatts at the company's Belleville, Michigan, data center and 6 megawatts at its IA01 data center in Waukee, Iowa, plus more than 1,000 miles of new fiber. In February 2026 US Signal also bought a 70,000-square-foot Aurora, Illinois, building built for CNA Insurance, with plans to expand its capacity to 4 megawatts.

US Signal also operates smaller sites in Kentwood, Byron Center, Auburn Hills and Southfield, Michigan, none of them tracked here yet. In August 2026 the Indianapolis City-County Council voted 23-1 for a moratorium on new data centers through the end of 2027; it pauses new construction, not existing buildings like the Morenci Trail site.

Two large data centers are proposed on Edinburgh's western edge, and neither has permission. The City of Edinburgh Council refused Shelborn Drummond's plan for a data center of about 210 megawatts of power on the former Royal Bank of Scotland headquarters site at 1 Redheughs Avenue, South Gyle, and the developer appealed to the Scottish Government. In August the government put the appeal on hold until Shelborn Drummond submits a full environmental impact assessment. No appeal decision has been published.

Councilors on the development management sub-committee refused the South Gyle plan unanimously in early February 2026, although the council's planning officers had recommended approval. They doubted the project's "green" label: committee papers projected about 200,000 metric tons of emissions a year, and the plan would remove a quarter of the trees on the site. "If this isn't a green data centre, which I believe it isn't, there are major issues with this proposal," said Green councilor Alys Mumford. The campaign group Action to Protect Rural Scotland warned the backup generators could burn the equivalent of "100,000 idling cars-worth of diesel."

The second project is a 200-megawatt data center at Hermiston proposed by Apatura. The council acknowledged its pre-application notice in March 2026, and the Scottish Government has ruled that it needs a full environmental impact assessment, Deadline News reported on September 15.

Barcelona's newest large data center is MERLIN Edged's building in the Zona Franca logistics park, which opened on May 13, 2025 with CoreWeave, a U.S. AI cloud company, as its tenant. The first phase uses 15 megawatts of power and holds 10,224 Nvidia H200 chips; CoreWeave planned a second phase with newer Nvidia Blackwell chips in 2026. Mayor Jaume Collboni opened it and called it "un projecte estratègic" (a strategic project) for the Zona Franca.

The operators say the building uses no water for cooling and runs on renewable power; the local broadcaster betevé reported it created 60 jobs. It connects to the Barcelona Cable Landing Station, where undersea internet cables come ashore.

Not everyone in the city shares the mayor's enthusiasm. On September 22, 2026, the campaign "No als megacentres de dades a Catalunya" protested outside the opening of the AI Summit Barcelona, presenting a manifesto it says more than 140 groups have signed. It wants a moratorium on data centers above 5 megawatts across Catalonia until there are rules for transparency and public oversight.

The Nordic data center company atNorth plans a data center of up to 300 megawatts at Hamre Industrial Park in Långsele, in Sollefteå municipality. The municipality has signed the sale of the roughly 50-hectare site for 175 million kronor, the zoning plan is final, and the site is due to start operating in the fall of 2028, the municipality said in May 2026. The next step is securing the environmental and building permits needed before construction starts.

In May 2026 atNorth and the grid company E.ON Energidistribution signed a deal for a 200-megawatt power connection. That will need a new substation at Hamre and a roughly five-kilometer, 130,000-volt overhead line to the national grid station at Nässe. Cooling methods and water use will be tested in an environmental review handled by the county administrative board.

The municipality expects about 100 to 150 permanent jobs, plus several hundred during construction, and sees a chance to put the waste heat to use. It argues that Sollefteå, one of Sweden's largest power producers, would use more of its own electricity at home, and says household power prices are set on the Nordic market and would not be directly affected.

County Mayo's one data center proposal was refused in mid-September 2026. An Coimisiún Pleanála, the national planning appeals board, overturned Mayo County Council's April 2025 approval of a 50-megawatt data center outside Killala, proposed by Mayo Data Hub Ltd, part of the US firm Avaio Digital. The refusal can only be challenged by judicial review in the courts, filed within eight weeks of the decision being formally published, which puts the deadline around mid-November.

The board said the developer had not shown it had a firm grid connection, enough local power capacity or any deal to buy renewable power, and that the plan clashed with Ireland's Climate Action Plan 2025. "The proposed development is considered to be premature in the absence of this detail," it ruled. The appeal was brought by Colin Doyle of Ennis, County Clare. The novelist Sally Rooney, a Mayo resident, had objected to the council, saying the power demand would add to the "catastrophic planetary crisis that is global warming."

Avaio had described the building of about 29,000 square meters as a €1.5 billion investment with 300 construction jobs and up to 35 permanent ones, placed in north Mayo because of its surplus wind power. Deputy Paul Lawless welcomed the refusal, saying data centers "are placing huge pressure on the grid." Minister of State Alan Dillon called it "disappointing news" for Killala and said he would take up the issues with IDA Ireland, EirGrid and Mayo County Council.

County Meath has two of Ireland's big data center sites, both running. Meta operates its Clonee data center at Portan, on the Dublin border, and in 2019 added two buildings that brought the site to nearly 150,000 square meters. Amazon Web Services runs a data center in the IDA Business and Technology Park on the Donore Road outside Drogheda, where it has planned three buildings that together would use no more than 144 megawatts of power.

Amazon's first Drogheda building was approved by Meath County Council in February 2020 with no objections. The council approved a second, 48-megawatt building in June 2021, but An Taisce appealed, arguing that councils approve data centers one at a time without counting their combined energy use. An Bord Pleanála granted it in April 2022, finding it would not significantly affect Ireland's climate targets. AWS put the worst case for all three buildings at about 473,040 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year.

At Clonee, which Meta says represents a €1.4 billion investment supporting more than 300 jobs, engineers in the Connect union held a 24-hour strike on October 7, 2024, over new shift patterns that they said meant more weekends and nights. In March 2025 Meta proposed cutting 14 jobs at the site.

Hamilton County's one mapped data center is Expedient's IND1 at 701 Congressional Boulevard in Carmel, an operating building that rents computer space and cloud services to businesses. It has 53,000 square feet, 26,000 of it server floor, and is built for 4.4 megawatts of computer power, with 8 megawatts of backup generators, according to the company. That is small next to the campuses being fought over elsewhere in Indiana, which run to hundreds of megawatts.

The one data center on record in Boone County is CyrusOne's CIN6 in Florence, an existing building close to downtown Cincinnati and the Cincinnati airport. It is already operating, so there is no pending vote or hearing on it. The building is 143,000 square feet, with 55,000 square feet of computer rooms and 5 megawatts of power for its computers, according to CyrusOne.

CyrusOne rents space in the building to businesses for their computer servers, backup and disaster recovery. The company says the site uses no water for cooling and only a little for humidity control and maintenance.

IREN, an Australian-listed company that runs bitcoin and AI computing data centers, has an Oklahoma campus in development near Carmen, at State Highway 45 and County Road 540 in Alfalfa County. IREN's own site lists the project at 1,600 megawatts of power across roughly 2,000 acres and says the power for it is already secured. The company has not said when construction will start or named a tenant for the site. No county hearing, vote, or local news coverage of the project has turned up yet.
Armstrong County has one data center on record: Ark Data Centers operates a 1-megawatt facility in Freeport, according to the company's own site. No larger data center proposal is on record here.
Nearby, Gilpin Township adopted zoning rules for data centers on April 23, 2026, ahead of any application being filed there. The rules remain in effect with no end date.

DC Blox runs a data center in Greenville's Global Business Park, off Interstate 85. The colocation company opened the facility in January 2022 after breaking ground in April 2021, and it is the county's only data center project on record.

The first phase covers 25,000 square feet and can hold more than 400 equipment cabinets on 3 megawatts of power. DC Blox has said the site could grow to 54,000 square feet and 18 megawatts of power at full build-out, though no expansion has been announced. "This first Tier III-designed data center in this market was built specifically to accelerate the deployment of critical infrastructure and interconnected cloud services throughout South Carolina," said Jeff Uphues, DC Blox's chief executive, when the facility opened.

Cipher Digital has proposed a 200-megawatt data center in Runnels County, called Ulysses. The company's own investor materials list an energization target of the fourth quarter of 2027. Cipher has not disclosed where in the county the project would sit.

Equinix and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board agreed in February 2026 to buy atNorth from its owner, Partners Group, in a deal with an enterprise value of $4 billion and a total financing package of $4.2 billion. CPP is putting in $1.6 billion for 60 percent of the company; Equinix takes the other 40 percent. This record holds the six atNorth sites already running or under construction under that deal: two in Denmark, two in Iceland and two in Finland.

The largest already operating is ICE02 in Keflavík/Reykjanesbær, Iceland, at 83 megawatts and expanding, next to ICE03 in Akureyri (12 megawatts) and DEN01 in Copenhagen (30 megawatts). FIN01/FIN03, in Espoo near Helsinki, is also operating. DEN02, a proposed 250-megawatt site in Varde, Denmark, and FIN04, under construction in Myllykoski, Kouvola, Finland, are still being built.
atNorth chief executive Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson said the company would "continue to operate independently under the atNorth brand" after the sale closes.

North Olympic Peninsula Data Centers runs a small colocation facility at 213 West Patison Street in Port Hadlock-Irondale, the only data center site tracked in Jefferson County. It rents secure cabinet space starting at $50 a month, with one IP address and 1 megabit of bandwidth included, according to the company's website. The business is also listed as a local internet provider on the Jefferson County Public Utility District's business directory.

This is a working local colocation shop, not a large campus proposal, so there is no megawatt figure to report and no public vote pending. Residents with questions can reach the company at 360-385-4686.

Rowan Digital Infrastructure, set up in 2021 by Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners and Birch Infrastructure, is building three campuses: Bauxite I, II and III at the Quantum Frederick data center park in Frederick County, Maryland, plus one each in Oregon and Texas. Frederick County's planning commission approved Bauxite II and Bauxite III in December 2024, adding to the 300 megawatt Bauxite I development that had already broken ground.

Water is central there. Quantum Frederick sits on the former Alcoa Eastalco aluminum plant, a brownfield site; Bauxite I and II each need 392,000 gallons of water a day for cooling and Bauxite III needs 297,000, and those totals used up nearly all the water the county allows for the first phase of the wider 2,100-acre campus.

In Oregon, Rowan wants to rezone about 274 acres of farmland outside Boardman in Morrow County for the Percheron Data Center, four buildings totaling 1.1 million square feet; the company says the land has been vacant since the 1950s and had no confirmed tenant when the county planning commission recommended approval. In Texas, Rowan's Cinco campus near San Antonio in Medina County broke ground in 2025 and closed $550 million in construction financing in February 2026 for the first phase of a planned 300 megawatt, 440-acre site, with the first 60 megawatts due online in 2026.

Maquoketa ended early talks about a data center on 46 acres in its South Highway 61 Industrial Park on August 18, 2026. The developer had not filed a formal plan, and city officials said no employee or council member signed a nondisclosure agreement over the discussions.
The industrial land remains available for other projects. City Manager Josh Boldt said Maquoketa will review its heavy industrial zoning language before another data center proposal arrives.

Provident Realty Advisors withdrew two data center applications in Porter County, Indiana, after local opposition. In Chesterton, the company pulled a proposed $1.3 billion, eight-building campus on a former golf course in June 2024. Town council members had said they could not support the plan at its proposed size and location.

Provident then sought a seven-building campus on 102 acres of Worthington Steel land in Burns Harbor. It withdrew that application in October 2024 but said it might return with changes. By February 2025, the town had heard nothing further. Residents had objected to the proposed building heights, setbacks and noise.

In Hillsboro, Texas, Provident is seeking to buy about 300 acres north of the city from its economic development corporation for a data center. Residents raised concerns at an April 2026 meeting, and the corporation extended the presale contract for more due diligence.

Equinix's SY9x facility is in Rosehill, near Parramatta in western Sydney. It is the company's first xScale data center in Sydney and currently has more than 14 MW of power capacity. Equinix says the site will have more than 28 MW when fully built out.
SY9x is a three-story facility with redundant power and cooling systems. Equinix lists 30 hours of generator autonomy for the site.
Equinix operates its BR1 data center in Brisbane's Fortitude Valley. The facility offers 8,956 square feet of colocation space in a two-story reinforced concrete building.
Equinix lists redundant UPS power and cooling systems for BR1. Its facility information gives 30 hours of generator autonomy.

Meta opened its Odense data center in 2019 after announcing the project in 2017. The original building covered 55,000 square meters, and the campus was connected to a district heating system that can use waste heat from its servers.
Meta later planned two more buildings totaling 90,000 square meters. In December 2022, it said it would end work on those two buildings while continuing to operate its existing Odense data center.
Equinix's BX1 facility is a data center in Bordeaux with 5,554 square feet of colocation space. Equinix describes it as the city's first carrier-neutral data center and says it uses renewable energy.

The single-story building has redundant power and cooling systems, according to Equinix. The company lists 30 hours of generator autonomy and offers connections to its Paris data center network through Equinix Fabric.
CyrusOne's PAR1 data center is in a pre-existing industrial building in Wissous, Essonne. Its first phase is operating with 4.5 MW of IT capacity in one data hall.

CyrusOne plans 27 MW across six halls when all three phases are complete. The second phase, designed for 6.9 MW, is not yet operating, and the third phase awaits environmental authorization and planning permission.

Segro proposed a 75 MW data center on a former H&M warehouse site in Le Bourget. Its plans called for three buildings and 33 backup generators. Residents and the new mayor opposed the project over its scale and potential effects on nearby homes and schools.

The previous mayor issued a building permit in March 2026, but the new mayor withdrew it in June. In July, a court refused to suspend that withdrawal, finding the proposed building exceeded local height rules. The project remained blocked at that ruling.
CloudHQ's CDG campus is in Lisses, south of Paris. The company plans two data center buildings, each with 74.4 MW of IT load, on a site served by a new on-site substation.
The first phase was inaugurated in June 2025. CloudHQ plans to send waste heat from the facility into the Corbeil-Essonnes district heating system, which could serve up to 7,000 homes.
Equinix lists its PA8x hyperscale data center in Pantin as a six-story facility. Its published specifications give 14,000 kVA of total sellable capacity and redundant power and cooling systems.

The same project record also groups PA9x, a separate five-story Equinix xScale facility with 9,600 kVA of listed sellable capacity. The facility pages do not give enough location detail to establish that both buildings are in Pantin.
Digital Realty lists three data centers on In der Steele in Düsseldorf: DUS1, DUS2 and DUS3. Their published building sizes are 47,500, 58,000 and 75,000 square feet, respectively.
The company describes all three as network-neutral facilities on European fiber routes. It says DUS3 hosts a core network node of the ECIX internet exchange.

Frankfurt has several data center sites in this record. Digital Realty's FRA20 is on Hugo-Junkers-Strasse and lists an 86,000-square-foot building. Equinix lists its FR1 facility on Taubenstrasse in central Frankfurt.

Equinix also describes FR9x and FR11x as two hyperscale facilities on its Northeast campus. Its facility pages list redundant power and cooling for both. The Iron Mountain FRA-1/FRA-2 row remains in the table, but its cited archive was unavailable for a sourced local description.
CyrusOne places its FRA5 data center campus in Hanau, near Frankfurt. The company lists 54 MW of IT capacity and 18,000 square meters of technical space in two three-story buildings.

Its specifications call for separate electrical plant serving each 9 MW data hall and dual redundant power supplies. CyrusOne also lists on-site engineering staff and a target of renewable power for the campus.
Digital Realty lists FRA33 at Mainzer Landstrasse 500 in Hattersheim am Main. Its facility page gives a total building size of 192,000 square feet and says the site is powered by renewable energy.
The company lists on-site security staff, camera coverage and biometric access. The project row groups FRA32 through FRA34, but this cited page establishes the details of FRA33 only.

Stack Infrastructure withdrew its plan for a data center on the former Continental site in Babenhausen in July 2026. The landowner, Aumovio, cited a long and uncertain planning process and said it would seek another investor for the site.

The project would have covered about 270,000 square meters. A coalition in the city council had asked for more information on renewable power, water use, noise and a financial guarantee before backing the plan.
CloudHQ's Frankfurt campus is in Offenbach am Main. The company lists two fully permitted buildings, each designed for 56 MW of critical IT load, and a 112 MW total for the campus.
CloudHQ says the site entered service in 2023. Its campus is served by an on-site substation, and the company has built fiber routes to two interconnection points.

Vantage describes a planned data center campus in Profile Park, Dublin. Its first two phases would provide two buildings with a combined 52 MW of critical IT load across 405,000 square feet. The company says the site has room for a third building.

The proposal includes an on-site 100 MVA generation plant designed to use hydrotreated vegetable oil and gas. Two separate Dublin data center planning appeals shown in the local wins table were refused: an application by Vantage Data Centres DUB11 in April 2025 and one by Digital Netherlands VIII for two buildings in February 2024. The cited records do not establish that either refusal is a decision on the Vantage campus described above.
Digital Realty lists its ROM1 data center at Via delle Testuggini 98-100 in Rome. The company's facility page gives a total building size of 21,500 square feet.
Digital Realty lists redundant power and cooling systems and 24-hour on-site security for ROM1. It describes the facility as a connection point for networks across the Mediterranean.
Digital Realty lists two data centers in Mombasa. MBA1 is on Mombassa Road and has a 10,500-square-foot building; MBA2 is on Kongoni Road and has a 27,000-square-foot building.
The company says both are near subsea cables that connect the region with other markets. Its facility pages list redundant power systems and on-site security for each.
Digital Realty lists NBO1 and NBO2 on Langata South Road and LRC Road in Nairobi. Their facility pages give building sizes of 15,500 and 12,000 square feet, respectively.
Both pages list redundant power and cooling systems. Digital Realty also lists security staff, camera coverage and controlled access at the facilities.
Digital Realty's AMS18 data center is at H.J.E. Wenckebachweg 127 in Amsterdam. Its facility page lists a 31,500-square-foot building.
The company lists redundant power and cooling systems, 24-hour on-site security and renewable energy for the facility. The page also lists a CarbonNeutral certification.

Digital Realty lists AMS3 and AMS11 in Schiphol-Rijk near Amsterdam's airport. AMS3 is on Cessnalaan and has a 56,500-square-foot building, while the AMS11 page lists Koolhovenlaan and a planned 111,000-square-foot building.

Digital Realty's AMS11 page says it will be operational in 2026, without confirming that it has opened. The project row groups several other AMS buildings, but the cited pages do not establish current status for each one.
Digital Realty lists its CT2 data center at 57 Tiber Road in Brackenfell, Cape Town. The facility page gives a building size of 319,500 square feet.
The company lists redundant power and cooling systems and on-site security for CT2. The tracked row also names CT1, but the cited CT2 page does not establish CT1's location or specifications.
Equinix describes MD3x as its first xScale data center in Madrid. The facility serves hyperscale deployments and has redundant power and cooling systems, according to the company's specifications.
A separate row lists Iron Mountain's MAD-1 in the Madrid area. Its only cited archive returned a request limit error, so no further local facts about MAD-1 can be verified from that source.

Khazna announced plans in April 2025 for a data center in Başkent Organized Industrial Zone outside Ankara. The company said the site could eventually reach 100 MW; its first phase was designed for cloud workloads, with scope to support AI later.

The proposed design includes solar panels, wastewater reuse and generators capable of using hydrotreated vegetable oil. Khazna said it planned to appoint a general contractor, but the cited articles do not confirm construction or an opening.

Khazna and BEEAH announced a joint venture in 2022 to develop a Tier 3 data center in Sharjah. They said the facility would have 9 MW of capacity once operational, with redundant power and cooling systems.

Equinix lists its AD1 data center in Abu Dhabi with 13,244 square feet of colocation space. Its facility page describes a two-story building with redundant power and cooling systems. A later Khazna announcement describes a separate proposed data center in Kalba, Sharjah; the cited articles do not establish that it is the same 9 MW project.
Equinix describes LD3 on Coronation Road in London as a data center and internet exchange point serving international businesses. Its facility page lists 29,063 square feet of colocation space.

The published LD3 specifications include redundant power and cooling systems and at least 30 hours of generator autonomy. The project row also groups LD1, but the cited LD3 page does not establish LD1's site details.
Equinix lists MA1, MA3 and MA4 data centers in Manchester. Its facility pages give 17,965 square feet of colocation space at MA1, 28,664 at MA3 and 12,949 at MA4.

The MA1 page places that facility at Manchester Science Park on Lloyd Street North, while the MA3 and MA4 pages list Reynolds House. All three pages describe colocation services and redundant cooling systems. The grouped project row also names MA2, which these cited pages do not establish.

Equinix lists LD11x as a three-story data center with 34,100 square feet of colocation space. Its published specifications include redundant power and cooling and at least 30 hours of generator autonomy.
Equinix also lists a separate LD13x facility for hyperscale deployments connected to its London Slough campus. Its cited page does not publish a street address or a power figure for LD13x.
Digital Realty lists LGW15 in Crawley, with a 66,000-square-foot building containing four data halls. The company's facility page gives its address as Power Avenue in the Manor Royal area.

Another Digital Realty row on this page is named Redhill, but its cited LHR20 facility page places the data center at 227 Marsh Wall in London's Docklands. The cited archive for Iron Mountain's London facilities returned a request limit error, leaving that row without a usable source for a local description.

Iron Mountain's PUN-1 data center sits in Hinjewadi, a tech district about 18 kilometers from Pune's airport in Maharashtra. The company says the facility opened in 2013 with 2 megawatts of power across 50,186 square feet, and connects to Iron Mountain's Mumbai site, MUM-1.

Greystoke's 90 megawatt data center plan for the former Woodlands Park landfill in Iver, Buckinghamshire, has no final decision. The UK government overruled Buckinghamshire Council's refusal in July 2025, but in January 2026 it admitted in court that the decision contained a "serious logical error" and agreed it should be quashed, after a legal challenge from Foxglove and Global Action Plan.

In April 2026 Greystoke agreed that its environmental mitigation measures must be made legally binding through a contract with the council, settling that part of the case. No new decision on the application has been reported since.
